title: Syllables
intro: Hard words split into syllables, then said whole. The stressed syllable is in capitals. Rate the four methods overall at the top, and each recording under its word.

cards.title: Directed: asked to split, then say it whole
cards.why: The hyphenated word and a bare director note in one Gemini request. The voice decides the rhythm, and may add a word or lose the split.
cards.notes: Rate the method overall, after listening to a few words.

cards.title: Markup: [short pause] between syllables
cards.why: The syllables joined with Gemini's pause tags, then [medium pause] and the word. The pause length is the voice's idea of short.
cards.notes: Rate the method overall, after listening to a few words.

cards.title: SSML breaks on the clear voice
cards.why: WaveNet, production's clear voice, reading SSML with an exact 300 ms `<break>` between syllables and 700 ms before the word. The most predictable of the four, and the flattest.
cards.notes: Rate the method overall, after listening to a few words.

cards.title: One natural take, cut and spaced
cards.why: The word said once, naturally, then cut at its loudness dips into syllables that are played with 250 ms between them, followed by the same take whole. The sounds are the real word's, and the cut can land in the wrong place.
cards.notes: Rate the method overall, after listening to a few words.

details.body:
You help build audio lessons for a language learner. In the lesson, some words are split into
syllables before being said whole — "a-tas-co … atasco" — so that the learner hears every sound.
Splitting costs time and gets tiresome, so it is only worth doing for a word that is genuinely
hard to say. Your job is to pick those words from a list.

The learner speaks English and is learning Spanish.

A word is worth splitting when at least one of these is true:
- **long**: four or more syllables, where a learner tends to drop or blur one in the middle;
- **stress**: the stress falls somewhere a English speaker would not expect;
- **cluster**: a run of consonants a English speaker struggles with;
- **sound**: a sound English lacks, such as a rolled r, a jota, a vowel with no
  equivalent, or a palatalised consonant;
- **spelling**: the spelling suggests a pronunciation that is wrong (silent letters, surprising vowels).

A word is not worth splitting just because it is rare, or because its meaning is hard. Short, plain
words never qualify. Most words in a list do not qualify, and picking too many is a worse mistake
than picking too few.

For each word you pick, give:
- `headword`, copied exactly from the list;
- `kinds`, one or more of `long`, `stress`, `cluster`, `sound`, `spelling`;
- `why`, one short sentence in English naming the exact difficulty, e.g. "Stress on -ve-, not
  per-", not "Hard to pronounce";
- `difficulty`: 1 (worth it), 2 (clearly helps), 3 (a learner will almost certainly get it wrong).

Answer with a JSON object and nothing else:

{"picks": [{"headword": "...", "kinds": ["..."], "why": "...", "difficulty": 2}]}

cards.title: el ayuntamiento · Spanish
cards.why: Chosen by hand: Five syllables with a diphthong in the middle that is easy to split wrongly: a-yun-ta-MIEN-to.
cards.facts: el·a·yun·ta·MIEN·to — the y sounds like a y-consonant

cards.facts: la·pre·dis·po·si·CIÓN — the n is nasal

cards.title: imprescindible · Spanish
cards.why: Chosen by hand: Two clusters, mpr and sc, one after the other.
cards.facts: im·pres·cin·DI·ble — the b is soft

cards.why: Chosen by hand: fr, then an i-a that belongs to one syllable, not two.
cards.facts: es·ca·lo·fria·TE — the i is unstressed in the dipthong ⚠ The syllables do not join back to the word.
